::: {.pageinfo}
Builds on [page 4, the violin string](violin.qmd) and the loop of [page 3](circle.qmd). Math: up to Bessel functions (described). About 3 minutes for the summary; about 35 with the mathematics.
:::

::: {.puzzle}
A drumhead is a sheet pulled tight: a string with a second dimension. Pluck a string and you get a note you could hum. Strike a drum and you get a thud. What changes when the string becomes a sheet?
:::

The short answer: an ideal, uniform head has its frequencies off the lines, so it thuds; drums with a clear note, such as the timpani (kettledrums), are built so that one set of modes lands near the lines and the rest are weak or fade fast ([stage 5](#one-drumhead-two-drums)).

Listen first: tap the head anywhere, then tap dead center and compare.

::: {.newidea}
**In one sentence.** An ideal drumhead's frequencies (1, 1.59, 2.14, … times the lowest) fit no pitch, so a plain drum thuds; on a kettledrum, the air the head pushes pulls one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, a note.
:::

::: {.gist}
**The recipe on this instrument, in brief.**

1. *Newton's law* on a small patch of the head: tension pulls each point toward the average height of the points around it.
2. *The operator* is the two-dimensional version of the string's, $-c^2\Delta$, with the rim held still.
3. *Its spectrum*, for a round drum, comes from the zeros of Bessel functions: frequencies at 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, … the lowest.
4. *On the diagram*: those stems fall between the whole-number lines; no base frequency in the range we hear as pitch puts them all on or near lines.
5. *What we hear*: a sound that doesn't repeat at any rate we hear as pitch, and fades fast: a thud. Where you strike changes how loud each mode is, never where it sits. A kettledrum's surroundings move one set of modes near the lines: a note.

[Skip to what we hear](#what-we-hear) if you only want the answer.
:::

## 1 · Newton's law: the equation of motion

*Mathematics used: partial derivatives, integrals over an area, the divergence theorem and polar coordinates (quoted), and Bessel functions (described, computed numerically).*

Here is where the drum's frequencies come from. Apply Newton's law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one small patch of the drumhead. The steps are the string's, with one more dimension.

**1. One small patch.** Let $u(x, y, t)$ be the height of the head above its rest position at the point $(x, y)$ at time $t$; subscripts are [partial derivatives](glossary.qmd#partial-derivative). The head has mass $\sigma$ per unit area, and its tension $T$ is a force per unit length of any cut through it. Take any small patch $D$ of the head. Its mass is the sum of $\sigma\,dA$ over its tiny area pieces $dA$; the double integral $\iint_D$ below means exactly that, adding up over all the small pieces $dA$ of $D$. So Newton's law for its up-and-down motion reads
$$
\iint_D \sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA = \text{net force on the patch}.
$$

**2. The pull across its edge.** Along each short piece $ds$ of the patch's edge, the sheet outside pulls with force $T\,ds$, along the surface and outward. If the head makes a small angle $\theta$ with the horizontal there, the upward part of that pull is $T\sin\theta\,ds$; for a small angle $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta$ (both are about $\theta$ in radians), and $\tan\theta$ is the slope. So the upward part is $T\,\partial_n u\,ds$, where $\partial_n u$ is the slope of the head in the outward direction across the edge. This is the string's step, with the slope taken across the edge.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
    <svg class="patch" viewBox="0 0 320 200" role="img" aria-label="A patch of the drumhead with tension pulling outward along its edge">
      <ellipse class="sheet" cx="160" cy="105" rx="90" ry="45"/>
      <line class="pull" x1="250" y1="105" x2="296" y2="88"/><path class="ph" d="M 290 82 L 302 86 L 293 95 Z"/>
      <line class="pull" x1="70" y1="105" x2="26" y2="118"/><path class="ph" d="M 32 124 L 20 120 L 29 111 Z"/>
      <line class="pull" x1="160" y1="60" x2="168" y2="18"/><path class="ph" d="M 162 22 L 169 10 L 174 23 Z"/>
      <line class="pull" x1="160" y1="150" x2="150" y2="190"/><path class="ph" d="M 145 184 L 149 196 L 157 186 Z"/>
      <line class="n" x1="250" y1="105" x2="300" y2="105"/>
      <text x="138" y="110">patch D</text><text x="256" y="128">T ds</text>
    </svg>
    <p class="cap">Tension pulls outward all around the edge. Where the sheet bulges, the pulls tilt and their vertical parts add up to a net force, which step 3 below works out.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

**3. Add the pulls around the edge.** The symbol $\oint_{\partial D}$ means adding up all the way around the edge $\partial D$ of the patch. Adding up the pulls around the edge turns into adding up one quantity over the inside of the patch. That is the [divergence theorem](glossary.qmd#divergence-theorem), quoted here, applied to the slope vector $(u_x, u_y)$: its outward part across the edge is $\partial_n u$, and its divergence is $u_{xx} + u_{yy}$. So
$$
T\oint_{\partial D} \partial_n u\,ds = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA .
$$
The quantity $\Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}$, the [Laplacian](glossary.qmd#laplacian), adds the second derivatives in the two directions across the sheet. In one dimension a patch is a segment, its edge is its two endpoints, and this step is the fundamental theorem of calculus, $u_x(b) - u_x(a) = \int_a^b u_{xx}\,dx$: the string's force again.

**4. Newton's law, at every point.** Steps 1 to 3 give $\iint_D \sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA$. This holds for every patch, however small, so the two integrands are equal at every point:
$$
\sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u .
$$
In words: on a string, tension pulls each point toward the average height of its two neighbors; on a sheet it pulls each point toward the average height of all the points around it, and $\Delta u$ measures how far a point sits below that average.

**What we assumed.** Small slopes; a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves; no bending stiffness; no air; and no damping and no sound radiation, so the model's modes never fade, while a real head loses its energy to the air quickly. The air matters for real drums, as the timpani paragraph in stage 5 says.

## 2 · The operator

Dividing by the mass per unit area $\sigma$ puts the equation in the series' form $u_{tt} = -A\,u$: the force per unit mass is a fixed rule applied to the head's shape, and that rule is the drum's [operator](glossary.qmd#operator). The rim completes it: the rim is clamped, so $u = 0$ there. This is the drum's [boundary condition](glossary.qmd#boundary-condition).

::: {.result}
**The drum's operator.**
$$
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = -c^2\,\Delta,
$$
with $c^2 = T/\sigma$, acting on shapes of the head that are zero on the rim. In words: tension pulls each point toward the average of its surroundings, and the rim holds still.
:::

## 3 · Its spectrum

A [mode](glossary.qmd#mode) is a shape $X$ that the operator only rescales: $A X = \lambda X$, with the number $\lambda$ called its [eigenvalue](glossary.qmd#eigenvalue) (an eigenvalue of $A$, constant included). Released in that shape, the head keeps it and swings as $X\cos\omega t$, with $\omega = \sqrt{\lambda}$, at the frequency $f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi$. The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator's [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum). Writing $\lambda = c^2k^2$, the mode condition is
$$
-\Delta X = k^2 X
$$
inside the drum, with $X = 0$ on the rim and $\omega = ck$. For a round drum of radius $a$, it can be solved by splitting it into a problem around the center and a problem outward from it, a [separation of variables](glossary.qmd#separation-of-variables).

**1. A round drum calls for distance and angle.** Measure position by the distance $r$ from the center and the angle $\theta$. In these coordinates the Laplacian reads
$$
\Delta X = X_{rr} + \frac1r X_r + \frac{1}{r^2}X_{\theta\theta}.
$$
This is a standard change of variables, quoted here; it follows from the chain rule ([Laplace operator in polar coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_operator#Two_dimensions)). The $X_r/r$ term is there because circles around the center grow longer as $r$ grows.

**2. Split the shape into an around part and an outward part.** Try a shape that is a function of $r$ times a function of $\theta$, $X = R(r)\,\Theta(\theta)$. Substituting into $-\Delta X = k^2X$ and multiplying by $r^2/(R\Theta)$ gives
$$
\frac{r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R}{R} = -\frac{\Theta''}{\Theta}.
$$
The left side depends only on $r$, the right only on $\theta$. Change $\theta$ alone: the left side can't change, so neither can the right. So both equal one constant.

**3. Around the center: the loop of page 3.** Going once around the drum must bring $\Theta$ back to itself, so $-\Theta'' = m^2\Theta$ with $\Theta$ repeating every turn. This is exactly the loop's eigenvalue problem from the [circle page](circle.qmd): $m$ is a whole number and $\Theta = \cos m\theta$ or $\sin m\theta$. A mode with $m \ge 1$ has $m$ straight still lines through the center, like spokes.

**4. Outward from the center: Bessel's equation.** What remains for $R$ is
$$
r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0,
$$
*Bessel's equation*. It depends on $r$ only through $kr$, so its solutions are functions of $kr$. Of its two essentially different solutions, one, the [Bessel function](glossary.qmd#bessel) $J_m(kr)$, is finite at the center; the other becomes infinite there, which would take infinite energy, so it is not a free mode. $J_m$ plays the part the sine played on a string: it wiggles like a cosine or sine whose swings slowly shrink.


**5. The rim picks out the frequencies.** The rim condition $R(a) = 0$ says $J_m(ka) = 0$: $ka$ must be a zero of $J_m$. Writing $j_{m,n}$ for the $n$-th positive zero, $k = j_{m,n}/a$. The zeros have no closed form and are computed numerically; those of $J_0$ are 2.405, 5.520, 8.654, …, in the ratios 1 : 2.30 : 3.60.

::: {.result}
**The round drum's spectrum.** Modes $J_m(j_{m,n}\,r/a)\cos m\theta$ and $J_m(j_{m,n}\,r/a)\sin m\theta$, for $m = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ and $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, with frequencies
$$
f_{m,n} = \frac{c\,j_{m,n}}{2\pi a}.
$$
In order, relative to the lowest: 1, 1.593, 2.136, 2.295, 2.653, 2.917, … Each frequency with $m \ge 1$ belongs to two modes, the cosine and the sine, the same pattern turned. The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_{m,n} = c^2 j_{m,n}^2/a^2$.
:::

These are all the modes: expanding any mode in a Fourier series in $\theta$ (page 3) reduces $-\Delta X = k^2X$, term by term, to Bessel's equation for each $m$.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Why the pairs are exact, and how the zeros are spaced</summary>

Each frequency with $m \ge 1$ belongs to exactly two modes because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders never share a positive zero; this was conjectured by Bourget and proved by Carl Ludwig Siegel in 1929. This page computes the zeros numerically. For large $n$ they approach $j_{m,n} \approx (n + \tfrac m2 - \tfrac14)\pi$: evenly spaced for one fixed $m$, but shifted by an amount that depends on $m$. The round head's symmetry shows up as a [multiplicity](glossary.qmd#multiplicity) of 2.

</details>
:::

## 4 · On the spectrum diagram

These are the frequencies in your last strike, as multiples of the lowest: each stem is one $j_{m,n}/j_{0,1}$ from the result box of stage 3. After 1×, the next few, 1.59×, 2.14× and 2.30×, sit between the lines. Higher up the stems crowd together, so some land near a line by chance, such as 2.92× and 4.06×; but no base frequency in the range we hear as pitch puts them all on or near lines. Each stem's height is how strongly that mode sounds at the listening ring for the strike you made: strike somewhere else and the heights change, never the positions. Tap a stem to see that mode on the drumhead and hear it alone.

## 5 · What we hear {#what-we-hear}

**Off the lines and fading fast: a thud.** The frequencies of stage 3 don't sit at whole-number multiples of any base frequency we hear as pitch, so the sound doesn't repeat at any such rate; and a real head gives its energy to the air quickly, so it fades fast. Together, a thud.

A struck head moves as the sum of its modes, $u = \sum a_{m,n} X_{m,n} e^{-t/\tau_{m,n}} \cos(2\pi f_{m,n} t + \phi_{m,n})$, each with its own fading time $\tau_{m,n}$ (damping, added to the model), so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies of stage 3; the drum demo at the top synthesizes it exactly this way.

**Why the frequencies miss the lines.** The frequencies are the zeros of the Bessel functions, scaled. For the modes with no spokes, the zeros of $J_0$ come at nearly even steps, about $\pi$ apart, but the first one is short, about $0.77\pi$ rather than $\pi$, so the later zeros are not multiples of the first: the frequencies go 1 : 2.30 : 3.60. Each number of spokes gives its own sequence, shifted by a different amount, and the sequences interleave at unrelated places. Merged, they give the drum's list 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, 2.65×, 2.92×, …, scattered between the lines. One more pattern: every mode with spokes comes in a pair, the same pattern turned, with exactly the same frequency. That is the round drum's symmetry, heard in its spectrum.

**The sand draws the still lines.** In 1808 Ernst Chladni showed the French Institute in Paris, the body that then held the Academy of Sciences, a trick: sprinkle sand on a metal plate, draw a violin bow along its edge, and the sand leaps into a pattern, a different one for each note. The sand is jostled wherever the plate moves and comes to rest where it doesn't, so each pattern is one mode's still lines. Here is the same trick on a drumhead: pick a frequency and watch where the sand goes.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <canvas id="sCanvas" style="height:320px" aria-label="Sand on a vibrating drumhead gathering where the head stays still"></canvas>
  <div class="controls" id="sModes" role="group" aria-label="Which note to drive the drumhead at"></div>
  <div class="controls"><button id="sShake" class="primary">Sprinkle fresh sand</button><button id="sHear">Hear this note</button></div>
  <div class="readout" id="sRead"></div>
  <p class="cap">Each button drives the drumhead at one of its own frequencies, given as a multiple of the lowest. Every grain is jostled in proportion to how much the head moves under it, so grains drift until they reach a place where the head stays still. Chladni used stiff metal plates, whose operator involves bending, not tension; the sand behaves the same way on both.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

Napoleon offered a prize for explaining the patterns. Sophie Germain won it in 1816, the first woman to receive the Paris Academy's grand prize in mathematics, with a theory that was still incomplete; Gustav Kirchhoff gave the full theory of vibrating plates, with the correct edge conditions, in 1850. Finding the still lines and finding the frequencies are one problem: on a drumhead, the one on this page; on a plate, the same problem with the plate's own operator.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>Where the sand collects <span class="needs">uses polar coordinates</span></summary>

The mode $J_m(kr)\cos m\theta$ with $k = j_{m,n}/a$ is zero where $\cos m\theta = 0$, at $2m$ angles, which pair up into $m$ lines through the center, and along the circles where $J_m(kr) = 0$ inside the rim, $n - 1$ of them for the $n$-th zero. Those are exactly the lines where the sand collects.

</details>
:::

**Where you strike.** A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. Every mode with spokes stays still at the center, so a strike at dead center sounds only the round modes, those with no spokes; a strike on one of a mode's still lines leaves that mode silent. The two drums below use this.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>How strongly a strike excites each mode, in this model <span class="needs">uses integrals over an area</span></summary>

Number the modes $X_1, X_2, \dots$ in order of frequency. A sharp strike, a brief push at a point $p$, gives mode $i$ a starting speed in proportion to $X_i(p)$, the mode's height at the point struck, the same rule as the piano's hammer on page 7. We model what you hear as the speed of the head at a listening point $q$, which picks up mode $i$ in proportion to $X_i(q)$. Dividing by $\iint X_i^2\,dA$, the integral of the mode's square over the head, removes the arbitrary size of each shape. So mode $i$ sounds with weight $X_i(p)\,X_i(q)\big/\iint X_i^2\,dA$. (A real drum radiates sound from its whole head, and some modes radiate better than others; this model ignores that.)

</details>
:::

[]{#one-drumhead-two-drums}**One drumhead, two drums.** A bass drum and a kettledrum, one of the timpani, both start from this operator, yet one booms and the other plays a note. Three things separate them, where the head is struck, what surrounds it, and which modes fade first; step through them below. On the kettledrum, the air the head must push pulls the *spoke modes*, those with one or more lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim, close to 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a common base (HyperPhysics; Fletcher and Rossing), and the strike point and the fast fading of the round modes leave mostly those. Players and acousticians name the note at the lowest of them, the (1,1) mode, the drum's "principal tone" (Vienna's Institute of Musical Acoustics); the next sit a [fifth](glossary.qmd#octave), an octave and a major tenth (an octave plus a major third, ratio 5 : 2) above it. That is not quite what page 0's rule predicts: frequencies near 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a base nearly repeat at the base's rate, an octave below the (1,1), and HyperPhysics notes that the missing-fundamental effect might then give the drum that lower pitch. Which octave the ear names when a sound fits two pitches an octave apart is a question about hearing rather than about the drumhead, and this series doesn't settle it.

<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The toy model, the kettle, and other drums <span class="needs">uses integrals over an area</span></summary>

*Where each drum is struck.* A concert bass drum is played slightly off center; center playing, punchier and with less sustain, is kept for rhythmic passages (Graham 2017; Aleo, Interlochen 2023). There the spoke modes move little, so among the lowest modes the round ones dominate. Players muffle the head with a leg or a towel when the music calls for short notes, and let it ring for long ones (Aleo, Interlochen 2023); the step-through's Muffle button does the first. Timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out (HyperPhysics), roughly a third of the way in from the rim (Graham 2017). With the weight $|X(p)|\big/\big(\iint X^2\,dA\big)^{1/2}$ for a strike at $p$, on a head of radius 1, the lowest round mode (0,1) has 1.09 at the center, 0.73 at halfway and 0.37 at three-quarters, while the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) have between 0.74 and 1.19 anywhere from halfway to three-quarters: lower than the spoke modes' across the whole range. Nearer halfway the stick also sits close to the inner still circles of the modes (0,2), (1,2), (2,2) and (3,2), which lie between 0.44 and 0.65 of the radius, which quiets those too. The clear note also relies on the remaining modes being weaker or fading faster, which this page takes from measurements (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 18) rather than deriving.

*The air's mass.* Treat the air on both sides of the head as not squeezable, and each mode, locally, as a ripple of wavenumber $k = j_{m,n}/a$, whose crests are about $\pi/k$ apart. The air such a ripple sets moving reaches about $1/k$ from the head on each side, which adds a mass of about $2\rho/k$ per unit area ($\rho \approx 1.2$ kg/m³ for air) to the head's own $\sigma$:
$$
\omega^2 = \frac{T k^2}{\sigma + 2\rho/k}, \qquad f \propto \frac{k}{\sqrt{\sigma + 2\rho/k}} ,
$$
so coarse shapes, with small $k$, slow down most. This is the hub's [added mass](glossary.qmd#added-mass): it can only lower frequencies. A typical Mylar kettledrum head has $\sigma \approx 0.26$ kg/m², on drums of radius 0.32 to 0.355 m (Packer 1993); with $a = 0.33$ m, $2\rho a/\sigma \approx 3.0$. The spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) move from 1 : 1.34 : 1.67 : 1.98 to 1 : 1.42 : 1.83 : 2.24, halfway to 1.5 : 2 : 2.5. The rest of the shift comes from a full calculation of the air inside and around a finite head (Christian, Davis, Tubis, Anderson, Mills and Rossing 1984), not from the kettle's air spring, its uniform pressure.

*The kettle.* The nearly sealed kettle (it has a small vent) acts as a spring on the volume the head sweeps, $V = \iint u\,dA$, adding $\tfrac12\eta V^2$ to the stored energy for some constant $\eta > 0$. The operator gains the term $(\eta/\sigma)\,\mathbf 1\langle\mathbf 1, \cdot\rangle$, where $\mathbf 1$ is the constant shape and $\sigma$ the head's mass per unit area: a term of rank one. Every mode with $m \ge 1$ has $\iint X\,dA = 0$, because $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0$, so $\big(A + (\eta/\sigma)\,\mathbf 1\langle\mathbf 1, \cdot\rangle\big)X = AX$, and in this model it keeps its frequency exactly. Only the round modes are raised, and since the new term couples them to each other, their shapes change too; the explorable treats each on its own. The hub's [principle](spectrum.qmd#how-the-instrument-is-held-is-part-of-the-operator) says the same in general: added stiffness never lowers a frequency.

*The bass drum's second head.* A bass drum has a head on each end of its shell, coupled through the air inside, which splits its two lowest modes, (0,1) and (1,1); the two heads' lowest modes are commonly tuned about a fourth apart (HyperPhysics). Not modelled here.

*Other drums.* Toms are tuned to rough pitches, and a snare drum's crack comes from the wires, the snares, stretched across its lower head. The tabla and the mridangam reach near-whole-number overtones a different way: a patch of paste loads the center of the head, which makes the head's density non-uniform, outside this page's model (Raman and Kumar 1920; Raman 1934).

</details>
:::

## What we found

An ideal uniform drumhead, $A = -c^2\Delta$ with the rim held still, has its frequencies at the zeros of Bessel functions, 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, … the lowest: off the lines of the spectrum diagram, so a plain drum thuds. A kettledrum is the same head in different surroundings: the air it pushes pulls its spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, the strike point and the fast-fading round modes leave mostly those, and you hear a note. The next page turns the question around.

::: {.family}
**One operator family, as a first model.** Toms, snares, bass drums and timpani share this operator on a disk. They differ in tension, size and the mass of the head, and in what surrounds it, and the air in and around a drum changes the operator a little, or, for the timpani, enough to matter.
:::

## The next puzzle

Turn the question around: if you could hear every frequency a drum makes, could you work out its shape?

Short on time? This is the last page of the short path through the series, pages 0, 4 and 8. [Page 9](shape.qmd) takes it up, if you want more.

```{=html}
      sel = i; dspec(); var d = p[i].mode; solo = MODES.indexOf(d); soloT0 = performance.now();

      var pl = function (k, w) { return (k === 0 ? "no" : k) + " " + w + (k === 1 ? "" : "s"); };
      document.getElementById("dSel").innerHTML = "this mode: <b>" + d.ratio.toFixed(2) + "×</b> the lowest · " + pl(d.m, "still line") + " through the center, " + pl(d.n - 1, "still circle") + " inside the rim";
    } });
  }

  function frame(now) {
    var d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height;
    U.fill(0);
    var tv = (now - (solo >= 0 ? soloT0 : strike.t0)) / 1000, maxA = 0;
    for (var k = 0; k < K; k++) {
      var M = MODES[k], amp;
      if (solo >= 0) { if (k !== solo) continue; amp = C.reduce ? 1 : Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * Math.min(3, 0.5 * M.ratio) * tv); }
      else {
        if (tv > 8) continue;
        var c = RT[k][Math.round(strike.r * RN)] / M.norm, w = 2 * Math.PI * 0.55 * M.ratio;
        amp = c * Math.sin(w * tv + 1e-3) / M.ratio * Math.exp(-tv * (0.35 + 0.06 * M.ratio * M.ratio));
      }
      if (Math.abs(amp) < 1e-6) continue;
      var R = RT[k], cm = Math.cos(M.m * strike.th), sm = Math.sin(M.m * strike.th), CM = COS[M.m], SM = SIN[M.m];
      if (solo >= 0) { cm = 1; sm = 0; }
      for (var p = 0; p < GN * GN; p++) { if (INSIDE[p]) U[p] += amp * R[RI[p]] * (CM[p] * cm + SM[p] * sm); }
    }
    for (var p = 0; p < GN * GN; p++) maxA = Math.max(maxA, Math.abs(U[p]));
    var scale = solo >= 0 ? 1 / (maxA || 1) : 1 / 0.9, data = img.data, P = C.col["--pos"], N = C.col["--neg"], B = C.col["--panel"];
    if (solo < 0) { if (!frame.peak || tv < 0.05) frame.peak = 0; frame.peak = Math.max(frame.peak, maxA); scale = 1 / (frame.peak || 1); }
    for (var p = 0; p < GN * GN; p++) {
      var o = 4 * p; if (!INSIDE[p]) { data[o + 3] = 0; continue; }
      var v = U[p] * scale, c = v >= 0 ? P : N, a = Math.min(1, Math.abs(v));
      data[o] = B[0] + (c[0] - B[0]) * a; data[o + 1] = B[1] + (c[1] - B[1]) * a; data[o + 2] = B[2] + (c[2] - B[2]) * a; data[o + 3] = 255;
    }
    octx.putImageData(img, 0, 0);
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); ctx.drawImage(off, 0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--wood"); ctx.lineWidth = 6 * d; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(W / 2, H / 2, W / 2 - 3 * d, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.stroke();
    var lx = W / 2 + C.LISTEN.r * Math.cos(C.LISTEN.th) * W / 2, ly = H / 2 - C.LISTEN.r * Math.sin(C.LISTEN.th) * H / 2;
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.lineWidth = 2 * d; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(lx, ly, 7 * d, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.stroke();
    if (solo < 0 && strike.t0 > 0) {
      var sx = W / 2 + strike.r * Math.cos(strike.th) * W / 2, sy = H / 2 - strike.r * Math.sin(strike.th) * H / 2;
      ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(sx, sy, 5 * d, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill();
    }
    requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  }
  C.onTheme(dspec);
  dspec(); requestAnimationFrame(frame);
})();
</script>
```

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, cv = document.getElementById("sCanvas"), ctx = cv.getContext("2d"), G = 160, NP = 2600;
  var MODES = C.DR.slice(0, 10), sel = 3, grid = new Float32Array(G * G), px = new Float32Array(NP), py = new Float32Array(NP);
  function build() {
    var d = MODES[sel], mx = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < G; i++) for (var j = 0; j < G; j++) {
      var x = 2 * (i + 0.5) / G - 1, y = 2 * (j + 0.5) / G - 1, r = Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y), v = 0;
      if (r < 1) v = Math.abs(C.J(d.m, d.j * r) * Math.cos(d.m * Math.atan2(y, x)));
      grid[i * G + j] = v; mx = Math.max(mx, v);
    }
    for (var k = 0; k < G * G; k++) grid[k] /= mx;
    var lines = d.m === 0 ? "no lines through the center" : d.m + " line" + (d.m > 1 ? "s" : "") + " through the center";
    var circ = d.n - 1 === 0 ? "no circles inside the rim" : (d.n - 1) + " circle" + (d.n > 2 ? "s" : "") + " inside the rim";
    document.getElementById("sRead").innerHTML = "frequency <b>" + d.ratio.toFixed(3) + "×</b> the lowest · still lines: " + lines + ", " + circ;
  }
  function amp(x, y) { var i = Math.floor((x + 1) / 2 * G), j = Math.floor((y + 1) / 2 * G); if (i < 0 || j < 0 || i >= G || j >= G) return 0; return grid[i * G + j]; }
  function sprinkle() { for (var k = 0; k < NP; k++) { var r = Math.sqrt(Math.random()) * 0.98, t = 2 * Math.PI * Math.random(); px[k] = r * Math.cos(t); py[k] = r * Math.sin(t); } }
  function step() {
    for (var k = 0; k < NP; k++) {
      var a = amp(px[k], py[k]), s = 0.035 * a, t = 2 * Math.PI * Math.random();
      var nx = px[k] + s * Math.cos(t), ny = py[k] + s * Math.sin(t), rr = nx * nx + ny * ny;
      if (rr > 0.97) { var f = Math.sqrt(0.97 / rr); nx *= f; ny *= f; }
      px[k] = nx; py[k] = ny;
    }
  }
  function draw() {
    var d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, R = Math.min(W, H) / 2 - 8 * d, cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2;
    if (!C.reduce) { step(); step(); }
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--wood", 0.25); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx, cy, R, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill();
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.lineWidth = 3 * d; ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--ink", 0.8); var g = 1.6 * d;
    for (var k = 0; k < NP; k++) ctx.fillRect(cx + px[k] * R - g / 2, cy - py[k] * R - g / 2, g, g);
    requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  }
  var box = document.getElementById("sModes");
  MODES.forEach(function (m, i) {
    var b = document.createElement("button"); b.type = "button"; b.textContent = m.ratio.toFixed(2) + "×"; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", i === sel);
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { sel = i; Array.prototype.forEach.call(box.children, function (c, k) { c.setAttribute("aria-pressed", k === i); }); build(); sprinkle(); });
    box.appendChild(b);
  });
  document.getElementById("sShake").addEventListener("click", sprinkle);
  document.getElementById("sHear").addEventListener("click", function () {
    var f = 150 * MODES[sel].ratio, b = C.render([{ f: f, amp: 1, tau: 20 }], 1.6), dd = b.getChannelData(0), n = Math.floor(0.25 * b.sampleRate);
    for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) dd[dd.length - 1 - i] *= i / n;
    C.play(b, 0.6);
  });
  build(); sprinkle(); requestAnimationFrame(draw);
})();
</script>
```

```{=html}
<script>
// One drumhead, two drums: a five-step toy model (bass drum above, timpani below).
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = window.Core;
  var J11 = C.DR.filter(function (d) { return d.m === 1 && d.n === 1; })[0].j, J01 = C.DR[0].j;
  var MODES = C.DR.filter(function (d) { return d.j / J11 <= 3.6; });
  function kind(d) { return d.m === 0 ? "round" : d.n === 1 ? "spoke" : "other"; }
  var COL = { round: "--pos", spoke: "--neg", other: "--metal" };
  var STEPS = {
    1: ["Same head, same operator", "Both drums start as this page's operator on a disk with the rim held still. On this ideal head the frequencies fall off the dashed lines, and the two diagrams are identical. Two kinds of mode will matter: the round modes, with no line through the center, and the spoke modes, with lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim."],
    2: ["Where you strike decides which modes start", "A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. A bass drum is struck slightly off center, where the spoke modes barely move, so its lowest modes are mostly round ones. A kettledrum is struck between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, where the lowest round mode starts more weakly than the spoke modes."],
    3: ["The air adds mass, most to coarse shapes", "Air on both sides of the head moves with it. A ripple of wavenumber k drags along a layer of air about 1/k thick, so a coarse mode carries more extra mass and slows down more: f ∝ k / √(σ + 2ρ/k). This happens to both drums. It stretches the spoke modes toward the dashed lines; in this toy model it gets about halfway, and a full calculation of the air gets the rest."],
    4: ["What surrounds each head", "A kettledrum's bowl is nearly sealed, so its air resists only shapes that change the volume it encloses. A mode with lines through the center pushes up as much as it pulls down, sweeps no net volume, and keeps its frequency exactly; only the round modes are raised. A bass drum has no kettle: its second head, coupled through the air in the shell, splits its lowest modes instead (not modelled here)."],
    5: ["What fades", "A round mode pumps air like a piston and radiates its energy away within a fraction of a second. On the bass drum, a strike near the center starts mostly round modes among the lowest ones. How long the rest rings is the player's choice: a leg or a towel on the head muffles every mode under it, for short, dry notes (press Muffle); lift it and the drum rings on. The leftover stems that land near a line are chance near-misses of this toy model, not a set of modes pulled onto the lines, and a real bass drum's second head, coupled through the air in its shell, splits its lowest modes, which the model leaves out. The result is a boom with no clear pitch, as intended. On the kettledrum the spoke modes ring on, near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base an octave below the (1,1): a note. Real timpani sit closer to the lines than this toy model; press Measured ratios to see and hear them."]
  };
  var step = 1, rT = 0.62, MU = 3.03, KK = 1, RB = 0.15, MUFFLE = false;
  var drums = {
    bass: { kettle: false, spec: document.getElementById("tdSb"), head: document.getElementById("tdHb"), verdict: document.getElementById("tdVb"), disp: null },
    timp: { kettle: true, spec: document.getElementById("tdSt"), head: document.getElementById("tdHt"), verdict: document.getElementById("tdVt"), disp: null }
  };
  function rOf(D) { return D === drums.timp ? rT : RB; }
  // frequency of mode d with air loading mu and kettle kk (relative units)
  function omega(d, mu, kk) { var lam = d.j * d.j + (d.m === 0 ? kk * Math.pow(J01, 4) / (d.j * d.j) : 0); return Math.sqrt(lam / (1 + mu / d.j)); }
  function excite(d, r) { return Math.abs(C.J(d.m, d.j * r)) / Math.sqrt(d.norm); }
  function target(D) {
    var mu = step >= 3 ? MU : 0, kk = step >= 4 && D.kettle ? KK : 0, r = rOf(D);
    var w11 = omega({ m: 1, j: J11 }, mu, 0), hs = MODES.map(function (d) { return step >= 2 ? excite(d, r) : 1; }), hm = Math.max.apply(null, hs);
    // step 5: round modes radiate away; Muffle (bass drum only) damps every mode under the player's leg or towel, at any step
    return MODES.map(function (d, i) {
      var x = 2 * omega(d, mu, kk) / w11;
      if (D === drums.timp && MEASURED && d.n === 1 && d.m >= 1) x = d.m + 1; // the measured pattern, not this model
      return { x: x, h: hs[i] / hm, gone: (step >= 5 && d.m === 0) || (D === drums.bass && MUFFLE), d: d };
    });
  }
  var XMIN = 0.8, XMAX = 7;
  function drawSpec(D) {
    var cv = D.spec, dpr = C.fit(cv), g = cv.getContext("2d"), W = cv.width / dpr, H = cv.height / dpr;
    g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0); g.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var L = 8, R = W - 8, base = H - 22, top = 10;
    function X(x) { return L + (R - L) * (x - XMIN) / (XMAX - XMIN); }
    g.font = "12px IBM Plex Mono, ui-monospace, monospace"; g.textAlign = "center"; g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted");
    [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].forEach(function (x) { g.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); g.setLineDash([4, 4]); g.lineWidth = 1; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(x), top); g.lineTo(X(x), base); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]); g.fillText(x + "×", X(x), base + 16); });
    g.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(L, base); g.lineTo(R, base); g.stroke();
    D.disp.forEach(function (p) {
      if (p.x < XMIN || p.x > XMAX || p.h < 0.01) return;
      var hh = (base - top) * p.h;
      g.strokeStyle = C.rgb(COL[kind(p.d)]); g.lineWidth = W < 420 ? 3 : 4; g.lineCap = "round";
      if (p.gone > 0.5) { g.lineWidth = 1.5; g.setLineDash([3, 3]); }
      g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(p.x), base); g.lineTo(X(p.x), base - hh); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]);
    });
  }
  function drawHead(D) {
    var cv = D.head, dpr = C.fit(cv), g = cv.getContext("2d"), W = cv.width / dpr, H = cv.height / dpr;
    g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0); g.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R = Math.min(W, H) / 2 - 6, r = rOf(D);
    g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--paper"); g.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); g.lineWidth = 2; g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx, cy, R, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.fill(); g.stroke();
    if (D.kettle) { g.setLineDash([3, 3]); g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx, cy, R * 0.9, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]); }
    if (step >= 2) {
      g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx + r * R, cy, 5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.fill();
      g.font = "11px IBM Plex Sans Condensed, system-ui, sans-serif"; g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); if (r < 0.4) { g.textAlign = "center"; g.fillText("strike", cx + r * R, cy - 9); } else { g.textAlign = "right"; g.fillText("strike", cx + r * R - 8, cy + 4); }
    }
  }
  var GAL = MODES.slice(0, 10);
  function drawGallery() {
    var cv = document.getElementById("tdGal"), dpr = C.fit(cv), g = cv.getContext("2d"), W = cv.width / dpr, H = cv.height / dpr;
    g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0); g.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var n = W < 420 ? 5 : 10, rows = W < 420 ? 2 : 1, cw = W / n, rh = H / rows, R = Math.max(4, Math.min(cw, rh - 18) / 2 - 3), S = 2 * Math.ceil(R);
    var pr = C.col["--ink"], nr = C.col["--metal"];
    GAL.forEach(function (d, i) {
      var cx = (i % n) * cw + cw / 2, cy = Math.floor(i / n) * rh + R + 3, N = Math.round(S * dpr), img = g.createImageData(N, N);
      for (var py = 0; py < N; py++) for (var px = 0; px < N; px++) {
        var x = (px + 0.5) / N * 2 - 1, y = (py + 0.5) / N * 2 - 1, rr = Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y), o = 4 * (py * N + px);
        if (rr > 1) { img.data[o + 3] = 0; continue; }
        var v = C.J(d.m, d.j * rr) * Math.cos(d.m * Math.atan2(y, x)), c = v >= 0 ? pr : nr, a = Math.min(1, Math.abs(v) * 2.6);
        img.data[o] = c[0]; img.data[o + 1] = c[1]; img.data[o + 2] = c[2]; img.data[o + 3] = Math.round(40 + 215 * a);
      }
      var off = document.createElement("canvas"); off.width = N; off.height = N; off.getContext("2d").putImageData(img, 0, 0);
      g.save(); g.setTransform(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0); g.drawImage(off, Math.round((cx - S / 2) * dpr), Math.round((cy - S / 2) * dpr)); g.restore();
      g.strokeStyle = C.rgb(COL[kind(d)]); g.lineWidth = 2.5; g.beginPath(); g.arc(cx, cy, R + 1.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.stroke();
      g.font = "12px IBM Plex Mono, ui-monospace, monospace"; g.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); g.textAlign = "center"; g.fillText("(" + d.m + "," + d.n + ")", cx, cy + R + 15);
    });
  }
  function verdict(D) {
    if (step < 2) return "";
    var live = D.disp.filter(function (p) { return p.h > 0.15 && !(p.gone > 0.5) && p.x <= XMAX; }).sort(function (a, b) { return b.h - a.h; }).slice(0, 5).sort(function (a, b) { return a.x - b.x; });
    if (!live.length) return D === drums.bass && MUFFLE ? "muffled: a short note" : "everything fades fast";
    return "tallest stems at " + live.map(function (p) { return p.x.toFixed(2) + "×"; }).join(" · ");
  }
  var anim = 0;
  function render() {
    var done = true;
    ["bass", "timp"].forEach(function (k) {
      var D = drums[k], T = target(D);
      if (!D.disp) D.disp = T.map(function (p) { return { x: p.x, h: p.h, gone: p.gone ? 1 : 0, d: p.d }; });
      D.disp.forEach(function (p, i) {
        var q = T[i], gx = q.x - p.x, gh = q.h - p.h, gg = (q.gone ? 1 : 0) - p.gone;
        p.x += 0.18 * gx; p.h += 0.18 * gh; p.gone += 0.18 * gg;
        if (Math.abs(gx) > 1e-3 || Math.abs(gh) > 1e-3 || Math.abs(gg) > 1e-3) done = false; else { p.x = q.x; p.h = q.h; p.gone = q.gone ? 1 : 0; }
      });
      drawSpec(D); drawHead(D); D.verdict.textContent = verdict(D);
    });
    anim = done ? 0 : requestAnimationFrame(render);
  }
  function kick() { if (!anim) anim = requestAnimationFrame(render); }
  var btns = document.querySelectorAll("#td [data-td]");
  function setStep(s) {
    step = s;
    Array.prototype.forEach.call(btns, function (b) { b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", +b.getAttribute("data-td") === s ? "true" : "false"); });
    document.getElementById("tdT").textContent = s + " · " + STEPS[s][0];
    document.getElementById("tdX").textContent = STEPS[s][1];
    if (C.reduce) { drums.bass.disp = null; drums.timp.disp = null; }
    kick();
  }
  Array.prototype.forEach.call(btns, function (b) { b.addEventListener("click", function () { setStep(+b.getAttribute("data-td")); }); });
  // Sound: each drum at its own size. The bass drum's lowest round mode sits near 50 Hz; the timpani's (1,1) is set to 130.8 Hz (C3).
  // From step 5 the round modes die within a fraction of a second, as they radiate their energy away.
  var MEASURED = false;
  function parts(k) {
    var D = drums[k], T = target(D), mu = step >= 3 ? MU : 0;
    var ref = k === "bass" ? 50 / (2 * omega(C.DR[0], mu, 0) / omega({ m: 1, j: J11 }, mu, 0)) : 130.8 / 2;
    return T.map(function (p) {
      var x = p.x;
      return { f: ref * x, amp: p.h * (step >= 2 ? 1 : 0.5), tau: p.gone ? (k === "bass" ? 0.25 : 0.07) : 1.6 / (1 + 0.03 * x * x) };
    });
  }
  function play(k) { C.play(C.render(parts(k), 3.5), 0.8); }
  document.getElementById("tdPb").addEventListener("click", function () { play("bass"); });
  document.getElementById("tdPt").addEventListener("click", function () { play("timp"); });
  var mf = document.getElementById("tdMuf");
  mf.addEventListener("click", function () { MUFFLE = !MUFFLE; mf.setAttribute("aria-pressed", MUFFLE ? "true" : "false"); kick(); play("bass"); });
  var mb = document.getElementById("tdM");
  mb.addEventListener("click", function () { MEASURED = !MEASURED; mb.setAttribute("aria-pressed", MEASURED ? "true" : "false"); kick(); if (MEASURED) play("timp"); });
  function bind(id, fmt, set) {
    var el = document.getElementById(id), o = document.getElementById(id + "o");
    function upd() { set(+el.value); o.textContent = fmt(+el.value); kick(); }
    el.addEventListener("input", upd); o.textContent = fmt(+el.value);
  }
  bind("tdR", function (v) { return v.toFixed(2); }, function (v) { rT = v; });
  bind("tdMu", function (v) { return v.toFixed(2); }, function (v) { MU = v; });
  bind("tdK", function (v) { return v.toFixed(2); }, function (v) { KK = v; });
  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { drawGallery(); kick(); });
  C.onTheme(function () { drawGallery(); kick(); });
  setStep(1); drawGallery();
  if (document.fonts && document.fonts.ready) document.fonts.ready.then(function () { drawGallery(); kick(); });
})();
</script>
```
